t: Why we're here: my story, and the story of Craveiral
s: Hello, I'm Pedro. And if you're watching this, it's because you're part of Graverell.
Maybe you started this week. Maybe you've been with us for years.
Either way, I want to start at the beginning. Because everything we do here, every decision we
make, every plate we serve, every bed we prepare, it all comes from one story. And I think you deserve
to hear it from me. Twenty years ago, I was a lawyer in Lisbon. I still am, actually. I never
stopped. But somewhere along the way, I realized that the life I was building was missing something.
I had the office, I had the career, I had everything that's supposed to add up to success.
And I kept dreaming about land, about farming, about getting my hands in the soil.
It sounds romantic when I say it now. Believe me, it didn't feel romantic when I was learning
how hard farming actually is. And then, one spring day, I found a field. A field of carnations
near São Teotônio, on the Costa Vicentina. In Portuguese, a field of carnations is a
Graverell. That's where the name comes from. It's not a marketing invention, it's literally what
the land was. I remember standing in that field and thinking, this is it. This is the place.
Nine hectares of wild Alentejo. Minutes from some of the most beautiful, unspoiled coastline in
Europe. No neighbors in sight. Sky so clear at night that guests still stopped me on the walkways to
point at the stars. That was 2010. We opened in 2018. Eight years. Let that sink in for a moment.
Eight years between the dream and the first guest. Eight years of licensing, of building,
of doubting, of running out of money and finding it again. Of convincing architects and engineers
and banks and, honestly, my own family. That a lawyer from Lisbon could build something real
in rural Odemira. Why am I telling you this? Not for sympathy. I'm telling you because I need you
to understand something fundamental. Graverell was not built to be a hotel. It was built to be
a relationship with a piece of land. The hotel is how we sustain that relationship. That order
matters. Land first, hotel second. When you understand that 100 small decisions we make
year suddenly make sense. Look at how the place is built. We have nine hectares. Do you know how
much of it is constructed? Four percent. Four. Everything else is farm, orchard, garden, pine
forest, open space. We could have built more houses. We could have made more money per square meter.
We chose not to because of the emptiness, the space, the silence at night that is the product.
Guests don't come here despite the fact that we built so little. They come because of it. The houses
themselves, 38 of them, are connected by raised wooden walkways. Have you ever wondered why we
built walkways instead of just paving paths? Because raised wood lets the land breeze underneath.
Water flows, plants grow, the soil stays alive. Even the way you walk to your house here
is a decision about respecting the land. Here's the phrase I want you to remember from this first
module. We say it in everything belong does. We do not own the land. We belong to it for a while.
Think about what that means for your work. If we own the land, our job would be to extract value
from it. Get the most out of it as fast as possible. But if we belong to it, then our
job is to leave it better than we found it. Better soil, better water, a stronger village,
a team that grows. Guests who live a little more connected to something real than when they arrived.
That's not a slogan for me. I gave up a quieter, easier life for this idea. And every person who
works at Creverell is whether you signed up for it or not. Part of that same idea now.
One more thing before we move on. People sometimes ask me, Pedro, was it worth it? Eight years?
All that risk? All that stress? And I always answer the same way. I've watched a child collect eggs
in the morning and run to show her parents like she'd found treasure. I've watched a couple get
married under our pine trees. I've watched people from the village find good, stable work five
minutes from home in a region where that is not a small thing. So yes, every single day it's worth it.

t: Our vision, our mission, and the chain
s: Welcome back. In this module I want to explain Belong.
You've seen the word on our materials, in our communication,
maybe on my email signature, Belong, giving shape to meaning.
And I know that, for some of you, it might sound like abstract branding words.
So let me make it very, very concrete.
Belong was born in 2012, as an idea before Graveral even opened.
It came from a simple conviction, and I want you to hear this sentence properly,
because it's the foundation of everything.
A place well cared for cares for those who inhabit it.
Say it to yourself.
A place well cared for cares for those who inhabit it.
It works in both directions.
If we take care of this land, this village, this region,
the land, the village and the region will take care of us.
Of our business, of our jobs, of our families, of our guests.
So, what is Belong in practice?
Belong is the signature brand that connects everything we do.
Graveral Farmhouse is the heart of it.
But there's also our beach bar, down on the beach, minutes from here.
There's the Mesa Ducam, our restaurant at the Gulbenkin Foundation in Lisbon.
There's our catering and events operation, which takes our table to houses, companies and celebrations.
And there's the shop and the laundry, which serve not just our guests, but the village of Santiago itself.
Different places, different teams, different customers.
One gesture.
And the gesture is always the same.
To bring those who eat closer to those who grow.
Now, our vision.
Every serious organization has one, and ours is exactly one line.
To regenerate the territory through a circular economy.
Let me unpack those two ideas, because they are not decoration, they're instructions.
Regenerate the territory, not preserve, not don't damage.
Regenerate.
That means actively giving back more than we take.
Soil that gets richer each year because we compost.
Water that gets recycled through the property.
Young people who can stay in Odemira because there's meaningful work here.
A food culture that gets stronger.
Because we buy from the shepherd, the fisherman, the winemaker, down the road.
When we say regeneration, we mean all of it.
Environmental, social, and economic.
The land, the people, the money.
All three have to get elsewhere together.
And circular economy.
This means the value we create goes around in a circle instead of leaking out.
The farm feeds the restaurant.
The restaurant's organic waste goes back to the compost, and the compost feeds the farm.
The hotel brings guests, the guests discover the region.
The region's producers sell to our kitchens and our shop.
The laundry serves the hotel and the village.
Money that comes into Craveral doesn't fly off to some headquarters far away.
It circulates here, in this territory.
That's the circle.
Every time you choose a local supplier, every time you send scraps to compost instead of the bin,
every time you recommend the village restaurant to a guest, you are turning that wheel.
Our mission then is what we do every day to serve that vision.
We provide a space where our community, including our guests,
can connect through agriculture, gastronomy, hospitality, and nature.
Notice the words connect.
We're not in the accommodation business.
We're not even in the food business, strictly speaking.
We are in the connection business.
A guest sleeps in one of our houses.
Fine, that's a bed.
But a guest who picks a tomato in the garden and eats it that evening at the farm table?
That's a connection.
A guest whose child feeds the animals in the morning?
Connection.
A guest who takes a bottle of local wine home
and tells the story of the vineyard at their dinner table in Berlin or Amsterdam?
That's the connection traveling onwards.
There's a phrase we use in belong that I want to teach you
because it should change how you talk about your own work.
We say the protagonist is the chain, not the name.
What does that mean?
It means that before the plate, there is a grower.
Before the room, there is someone who tended the land.
Before the wine, there's a family that's been making it for generations.
Our job, your job, is to tell that old chain.
The shepherd, the garden, the vineyard, the community.
Because that's where the value lives.
When a guest asks about a dish, don't just name it.
Tell them where it came from.
These courgettes were picked this morning, about 80 meters from where you're sitting.
I've watched guests face this change when they hear that.
It transforms a meal into a story they'll retell for years.
And notice what that phrase also says.
Not the name.
Not Craveral's name.
Not Belong's name.
Not my name.
We are not the heroes of this story.
The land is.
The producers are.
Our guests, when they connect with it, they are.
We're the ones who set the table.
So here's my ask from this module.
From today, when someone asks what you do, I'd love you to be able to say more than,
I work at a hotel.
You work at a project that's trying to prove that hospitality can heal a territory
instead of consuming it.
Whatever your role, kitchen, housekeeping, reception, farm, laundry, beach bar,
you are part of that proof.
Next module, our values.
Not as a poster on a wall, but as decisions you'll make this week.
Every company has values. Most of them live on a wall in a meeting room and die there.
I want hours to live in your hands, in the decisions you make when nobody's watching,
when the day is long, when the guest is difficult, when the easy choice and the right choice are not the same choice.
So let's go through them, not as a list to memorize, as tools to use, sustainability.
And I always insist on saying it fully, financial, environmental and social sustainability.
All three, in that unusual order, on purpose.
People are sometimes surprised I put financial first. Let me be honest with you about why.
If Craverell doesn't make money, everything else dies.
The farm dies, the jobs die, the mission dies.
The all-beautiful idea becomes a story about a lawyer who wasted his money on a dream.
Financial sustainability is what buys us the right to pursue everything else.
So when you avoid waste, when you take care of equipment, when you fill the washing machine properly,
when you upsell a wine you believe in, you're not being petty, you're protecting the mission.
Environmental sustainability you already know.
The 4% footprint, the water recycling, the composting, the regenerative farming.
And social aspect, fair work, local hiring, serving the village, being a good neighbor, three legs.
The stool stands on all of them, or it doesn't stand.
Simplicity.
This one is deceptive, because simplicity is hard work.
Anyone can make something complicated.
Look at our houses. Minimalist design, natural materials, nothing shouting for attention.
That's a thousand decisions about what to leave out.
In your work, simplicity means don't overcomplicate the guest's experience.
Clear answers, honest food, processes that make sense.
If you find yourself doing something convoluted and you don't know why, question it. Ask.
Maybe there's a reason?
Maybe it's just accumulated clutter and you found something we should simplify.
Comfort and modernity.
We are rustic in soul, but we are not a museum of rural hardship.
Our guests sleep on excellent mattresses.
The indoor pool is heated, the Wi-Fi works.
There are smeg appliances and we wood furniture in some of the houses.
And every house has a proper kitchen and a private terrace.
Why does this matter?
Because we are not asking guests to sacrifice comfort in exchange for authenticity.
The whole point of Craverell is that they get both.
Simplicity is not scarcity.
Remember that when you set up a room or serve a table, warm, generous, comfortable and simple.
Freedom and authenticity.
Guests at Craverell are free.
Free to do everything, surf lessons, horseback riding, hikes on the fisherman's trail, yoga or absolutely gloriously nothing.
Never make a guest feel they're missing out if they just want to lie by the pool for three days.
And authenticity means we don't perform.
The farm is a real farm. The eggs are real eggs from this morning. The people are real people.
You are not required to wear a corporate smile that isn't yours.
I would much rather a guest meet the real you with your real warmth and your real accent than some hospitality school character.
Guests can smell theater from a kilometer away.
What they can't resist is truth.
Creativity and community integration.
Creativity.
You're allowed to have ideas.
More than allowed, expected.
Some of the best things at Craverell came from the team, not from me.
And community integration.
We are of Santiago, not just in it.
The laundry serves the village.
The shop sells our neighbors honey and wine and olive oil.
We hire locally whenever we can.
When a guest asks what to visit, we send them to the village, to Odessage, to Zambugera, to the local restaurants.
We are ambassadors for the whole territory, not gatekeepers trying to trap guests on the property.
Well-being, and this one is for the guests and for you.
A burned-out team cannot deliver warm hospitality.
It's simply not possible to give what you don't have.
So take your breaks, eat properly.
Tell your manager when the load is too much.
Use the beauty of this place.
You work somewhere, people pay hundreds of euros a night to be.
Walk the property sometimes.
Look at the coastline on your day off.
If working here doesn't include some joy, we're doing it wrong, and I want to know.
Now, values are easy when everything's fine.
The test is when they conflict.
A guest wants something wasteful, comfort versus sustainability.
A creative idea costs money, creativity versus financial discipline.
I'm not going to pretend there's a formula. There isn't.
What I'll tell you is this.
When values collide, think about the long game.
We're not trying to win a day.
We're trying to build something that lasts decades.
The decision that serves the relationship with the guest, with the land, with the team.
Over the years, that's almost always the right one.
And when you're not sure, ask.
Asking is never a weakness here.
Next model, we get the craft itself.
Hospitality, the Cravey Rallway.
Let's talk about hospitality. The real thing, not the industry, the craft.
I want to start with a distinction that changed the way I think about this work.
There is a difference between service and hospitality.
Service is technical. The food arrives hot. The room is clean.
The check-in takes five minutes.
Service is measurable and it's mandatory. We must be excellent at it.
But hospitality is something else.
Hospitality is how the guest feels. Service happens to the guest.
Hospitality happens inside the guest.
You can have perfect service and zero hospitality.
We've all been to those hotels.
Floorless, polished, cold as a hospital corridor.
And you can have ample service with overwhelming hospitality.
Think of your grandmother's house.
The tablecloths might not be pressed,
but nobody in history has ever felt unwelcome at their grandmother's table.
Gravereal has to be both.
The standards of a great hotel and the feeling of a home.
Our welcome should say what our brand says.
Fica. Pertents. Stay. Belong.
So how do we do that, concretely?
First, guests are guests, not customers.
The word matters. A customer is someone in a transaction.
A guest is someone in your home.
When friends come to your house, you don't process them.
You open the door, you're happy to see them.
You offer them something to drink.
You make them feel that their arrival improved your day.
That's the posture.
Every arrival, every day, including the day you're tired,
including the arrival at 22 hours when you wanted to go home.
That family drove two and a half hours from Lisbon Airport,
probably with children asleep in the back seat.
Their holiday starts with your face.
Second, use names.
From the reservation, from the check-in, learn them.
Welcome back, Mrs Keller. How was the beach?
Costs nothing and is worth everything.
People spend their whole lives wanting to be recognized.
In a world of apps and QR codes and self-service kiosks,
a person who remembers your name is becoming a luxury.
We will always offer that luxury.
Third, anticipate.
The deepest hospitality answers needs the guest hasn't voiced yet.
It's cold tonight. Are the fire pits lit before someone asks?
A couple booked the owner's house for an anniversary.
Is there something waiting for them that says we noticed?
A child at dinner is melting down.
Can we bring the pizza a little faster without being asked?
Watch, notice, act.
Anticipation is just attention, plus initiative.
And both are free.
Force, know the land, tell the land.
Every one of you should be able to tell a guest where to watch the sunset.
Which beach suits small children?
Carvalal, by the way, easiest access.
And our beach bar is right there.
Where the fishermen's trail is most beautiful, what Medruño is,
and why they should try it.
You are not staff who happen to be in Alentejo.
You are the guest's connection to this territory.
That's the belong gesture, remember.
Bring those who eat closer to those who grow.
Every conversation is a chance to make that connection.
Fifth, the small rituals matter more than the grand gestures.
Guests forget the marble lobby of some five-star palace within a week.
What they remember for years.
The waiter who remembered which wine they liked on the second night.
The housekeeper who arranged the child's stuffed animals on the pillow.
The receptionist who printed the boarding passes without being asked twice.
Hospitality is compound interest.
Tiny deposits made consistently that add up to a feeling of being cared for.
Let me tell you what I consider the perfect crevary moment.
A guest once told me a check out.
And I've never forgotten it.
She said,
Pedro, the strangest thing happened to me here.
On the third day I stopped taking photographs.
I asked her what she meant.
And she said,
I realized I wasn't trying to prove I was here.
I was just here.
That's it.
That's the whole job.
Everything we do, the silence we protect at night,
the walkways through the trees,
the food from 80 meters away,
the fact that nobody is pushing an activity schedule at anyone,
all of it is engineered to help a human being arrive.
Not just check in.
Arrive.
In the deepest sense of the word.
Our guests live in cities under pressure on screens.
We give them back the rhythm of the land.
Sunrise, work, food, rest, stars.
When it works, it's not a holiday.
It's a repair.
And you, whatever your role,
you're a garden of that repair.
The housekeeper who works quietly while a guest sleeps late is protecting it.
The gardener who waves good morning is part of it.
The waiter who doesn't rush the table under the stars is honoring it.
One last thing for this model.
Worms is not servility.
We are warm.
We are generous.
We are attentive.
And we carry ourselves with dignity always.
You are professionals in one of the most meaningful crafts there is.
Taking care of human beings.
Walk like it.
Never grovel, never be cold.
Between those two extremes lives everything I mean by the word hospitality.
Next model.
The guest journey.
From the first click to the last look in the rear view mirror.

t: The guest journey: from first click to farewell
s: Every guest who arrives at Crevoral is on a journey that started long before the M501 brought them to our gate and finishes long after they leave.
In this module, I want to walk that old journey with you, stage by stage, because each of you owns a piece of it and it helps enormously to see the whole.
Stage one, the dream. Before anything, someone is at home, in Lisbon, in Munich, in London, scrolling, dreaming of a Skype.
They see our photographs, the houses among the trees, the long table, the coastline. At this stage, we've made a promise.
Everything our marketing shows, the aesthetics, the calm, the farm, is a promise that the operation, meaning you, will have to keep.
I take this seriously. We never promise what we can't deliver. Our photos are real, our words are real, which means the bar is exactly where it should be.
Reality has to match the dream. That's hard. That's also the job.
Stage two, booking and the time before. Someone chose us over hundreds of alternatives.
From that moment, they're already our guests, months before arrival. Every email answered quickly and warmly.
Every question about cuts or dogs or dietary restrictions handled with care builds their confidence that they chose well.
And remember, we favor direct bookings.
When guests book directly through creveral.pt, more of the value stays in the circle, and we can take better care of them.
When you talk to potential guests, that's always the best pass for them and for us.
Stage three, the arrival. Two and a half hours from Lisbon, 90 minutes from the Algarve.
Guests arrive tired, sometimes lost, often with kids who've had enough.
The first 15 minutes at creveral set the emotional tone for the entire stay.
I'd honestly say the first 15 minutes are worse than the next three days.
A genuine welcome. A cold drink. A calm, unhurried explanation of the house and the property.
Never a bureaucratic check-in. The message underneath every word and gesture must be, you made it.
You can let go now.
Stage four, the first morning.
This is where creveral really begins.
The guest wakes without an alarm for the first time in months.
Rosemary in the air.
Breakfast.
And our breakfast is a statement of identity.
Housemade breads, our preserves, local cheeses, eggs laid that morning, cooked how they want them.
The first morning is when the guest decides, mostly unconsciously, whether this place is what it promised.
Make the first morning perfect and the whole stay tilts toward joy.
Stage five, the days.
And here, the guiding principle is freedom.
Some guests want everything.
Surf at Carvalel, horseback riding on the coast, the boat on the Mirra River, hiking to Zambujera, yoga, massage, the thermal circuit on the wellness deck in the pines.
Others want the precise opposite.
Pool, book, wine, repeat.
Both are perfect stays.
Our art is reading which guest is which, offering without pushing, informing without pressuring.
And for families, the kids, pizza classes, the animals, the eggs in the morning, the bikes.
A child who feeds a goat at eight in the morning has already made the families holiday.
Children are not an inconvenience at Creveral.
They're the guests whose memories last longest.
Stage six, the friction points.
Let me be honest about where the journey typically strains because pretending otherwise doesn't help you.
Housekeeping timing, guests are out, guests are in.
Coordinating is genuinely hard.
Restaurant capacity on peak nights.
The distances on the property, beautiful, but a long walk with luggage in August heat, needs help offered proactively.
Weather, an Atlantic storm in April can bruise a beach holiday, and that's exactly when we shine or fail.
The heated indoor pool, the saunas, the fireplace, the long lunch.
A rainy day at Creveral should be remembered as the coziest day of the trip, not the lost one.
Know these friction points.
Own them before the guest feels them.
Stage seven, the farewell.
Departures matter as much as arrivals.
The psychology is real.
People remember peaks and endings.
Never let a departure be reduced to an invoice.
A warm goodbye, a genuine comeback, maybe something small from the shop or the farm for the road.
The last image in the rearview mirror should feel like leaving a friend's house.
Stage eight, after.
The journey doesn't end at the gate.
There's the review they'll write, and reviews are the modern word of mouse.
They decide whether the next dreamer in Munich clicks on us or on someone else.
There's the memory that ripens over months, and there's the return.
Our best guests come back year after year, and some have become genuine friends of the house.
That's the real measure of everything I've described.
Not whether they were satisfied, whether they'll be back.
Here's the mental exercise I want to leave you with.
Whatever your role, locate yourself on this journey.
Which stages do you touch?
Housekeeping touches four and five, every single day.
Reception touches nearly all of them.
The kitchen owns Stage Four's magic.
Maintenance quietly protects every stage at once.
Nobody at Creviral is outside the journey.
Once you see the map, you'll never again think of your work as tasks.
It's a relay, and the betton is the guest's trust.
Next module, the houses, the farm, and the standards we keep.

t: The houses, the farm, and the standards we keep
s: If you're going to represent Graveral, you need to know Graveral. Properly, in detail.
The way you know your own home. This module is a tour. Some of this, you know. I want
all of you to know all of it. Start with the big picture. 9 hectares. 38 independent houses
arranged in clusters, 3 main clusters of houses, plus studios closer to the central facilities.
Only 4% of the land is built. The rest is working farm, orchards, vegetable gardens, animals
and pine forest. All stitched together by those raised wooden walkways. The houses. Everyone
is independent. Minimalist but warm. Each with its own character. And all of them share
the same DNA. Sustainability, local craftsmanship, homage to Portuguese heritage. Every unit
has a proper equipped kitchen, organic amenities, air conditioning and a private terrace with
table and arm chairs. Pets are welcome. This matters to more guests every year. And we
do it properly, not grudgingly. Know your unit types. The studios. 40 square meters, sleep
2. The farmhouses, 64 square meters, one bedroom, sleep 4. The farm lofts, also 64 square meters,
sleep 2. We would the core in cherry and oak. And part of the crevice cluster, which has its own
private pool for its guests. The two bedroom houses, 85 square meters, sleep 4 comfortably,
up to 6. With the wood burning stove in the living room, the farmer's house, two bedrooms,
damp furniture, smeg kitchen, two outdoor decks and the owner's house. We would our signature.
85 square meters, Eston's mattress, cork bus, a small library. The house I'd show a magazine.
Why am I making you learn square meters and bedweeds? Because confidence sells. And vagueness
kills. When a guest asks, would the two bedroom work for us with the kids? The team member who
answers precisely, yes. And if the kids are small, the sofa bed in the living room gives you flexibility.
The second bedroom can be twins or a double. Tell me which. That person has just created trust.
Trust is the currency of this whole business. The shared spaces, three swimming pools,
the big outdoor one, 24 by nine meters proper laps. The heated indoor pool, 12 by five,
with the glass front sauna beside it. And the children's outdoor pool, the wellness deck
raised in the pine forest, outdoor sauna, hot tub, cold plunge, a real thermal circuit, the gym,
the nature interpretation center, wood and glass in the pines, which host yoga twice a week,
retreats, workshops, meetings and seats up to 50 for a banquet or 80 standing.
The terrace with the fire pits between the restaurant and the pool and the playground area,
which can host events up to 300 banquet style. The farm. This is not decoration and I need everyone
to internalize that. The farm provides most of what our kitchen serves. Over 70% of the
restaurant's ingredients are grown on site. Vegetable gardens, fruit orchards, herbs, free range
eggs. Guests are invited to walk it, to harvest seasonal produce, to meet the animals, to cook
what they pick in their own kitchenette if they like. Nothing is wasted. Everything is connected.
Field to fork, earth to plate, scraps to compost, compost to field. When a guest asks a farm question
you can't answer, that's fine. Walk them to someone who can and then learn the answer yourself
for next time. The shop, local wines, artisanal rums, small batch honey, jams, olive oil, herbal teas,
natural soaps and body oils made nearby with traditional methods. Comfortable clothing inspired
by farm life. The shop is the territory, condensed and portable. Every product has a story and a
producer. Learn a few of them. This honey comes from a producer 20 minutes from here,
turns a souvenir into a relationship. And the laundry in Sao Teotoniou, which serves our
operation and serves the village. I love that our back of house is also a service to our neighbors,
that circular economy in its plainest clothes. Now, standards. Let me tell you how I think about
them. A standard is a promise we've made to every future guest based on what we've delivered to past
ones. When housekeeping prepares a house, they're not cleaning a room. They're keeping a promise.
The guest paid for the crevirole of the photographs and the reviews. Every detail that's right,
the bed impeccable, the kitchen spotless, the terrace inviting, the amenities complete,
keeps the promise. Every detail that's wrong, breaks it. Just a little. And broken promises
accumulate silently. A guest rarely complains about the small stuff. They just quietly downgrade their
opinion. And then one day, they book somewhere else. And we never learn why. So my rule is simple.
Details are not small. In our world, details are everything. Because our all promise is care.
A farm hotel that preaches love of the land but has a dirty pool filter or a burnt out bulb on a
walkway is a contradiction the guest feels immediately, even if they can't articulate it.
Coherence between what we say and what we do is the highest standard we have.
And when you see something wrong that isn't your job, a fallen branch on a walkway,
a smudged window litter near the pool, there are two kinds of team members. The one who thinks
someone should fix that. And the one who fixes it or reports it within the hour.
Crevirole was built by the second kind. Be the second kind. Next module, the farm table and
everything we serve. The plate where the whole philosophy lands.

t: FarmTable: where the philosophy becomes food
s: If crevaryl has a soul, you can taste it, literally.
This module is about the farm table and about food,
which, if you know me at all,
you know is the part of this project
I could talk about for six hours instead of 10 minutes.
I'll restrain myself.
Let me start with the philosophy,
and it fits in one sentence.
Before the plate, there is a grower.
Everything else follows from that.
Over 70% of what we serve is grown on this property.
The vegetables ripened in our soil.
The herbs were cut this morning.
The eggs were laid today.
By hens, you can walk over and meet.
What we don't grow, we source as close as possible.
Cheeses from the region, fish from this coast,
wines from Alentejo,
and from the Vicentino vineyards up the road,
medroneo from the local distillery.
The menu rotates with the seasons
because the farm rotates with the seasons.
And that's not a limitation, it's the entire point.
A tomato in August here
tastes like a different food
from a supermarket tomato in January.
Our guests come, in part,
to remember what food actually tastes like.
This is what root to table means when we say it.
Not a marketing garnish.
A supply chain you can walk in five minutes.
Breakfast.
I said it before and I'll say it again.
Breakfast is a statement of identity.
Housemade breads, our own preserves,
local cheeses,
farm eggs cooked to order.
